I'm a data analyst in Milan. Day to day I work on **sales forecasting for home
appliances** at LG Italy: demand planning, sell-out data, and the gap between
what a model predicts and what a commercial team is willing to act on.

Before that I worked as a **research assistant on economic history**, building
datasets from primary sources: OCR of printed census tables, a crosswalk
reconciling Italian municipalities across the 1921 and 1951 censuses, and the
validation passes that turn scanned paper into something you can actually run
a regression on.

That job taught me the thing I keep coming back to: **most of the work is
upstream of the model.** By the time you're choosing between gradient boosting
and an ARIMA, the important decisions — what counts as an observation, what to
do with the gaps, which units are comparable across time — have already been
made, usually implicitly.

## How I work

I implement methods by hand before using the library version. Not out of
principle: a hand-rolled `SeasonalNaive` takes an afternoon and teaches you
exactly which assumptions the library is making on your behalf. It's the
cheapest insurance against an R² of 0.99 that means nothing.

I also write down where things failed. A portfolio of only successes tells a
reader nothing about judgment.
